games.name: Sound Dots
games.gpc_focus: Any GPCs a child has met so far — start with s, a, t, p, i, n words.
games.how_to_play: Write a short word (like 'pin') and draw a small dot under each single sound and a short line under each two- or three-letter team. The child touches each dot or line and says just that sound, then sweeps a finger under the whole word and says it all joined up. Cheer the moment the word 'pops' into a real word.
games.materials: A whiteboard or paper and pen. No printing needed.
games.players: 1 adult with 1 child, or a small group taking turns.
games.why_it_helps: Turns the abstract idea of separate sounds into something a child can point to and count.

games.name: Bolt the Robot Talk
games.format: blending robot-talk (original robot character, not any commercial mascot)
games.gpc_focus: Any taught GPCs — great for blending three- and four-sound words.
games.how_to_play: Bolt is a friendly little robot who can only talk in separate sounds because his voice box is a bit rusty. The adult is Bolt: say a word in its sounds in a wobbly robot voice, e.g. 'c... a... t'. The child is the robot mechanic who 'fixes' Bolt by blending the sounds and saying the whole word out loud. Then swap: the child is Bolt and robots a word for the grown-up to fix.
games.materials: Nothing, or a cardboard-box robot puppet if you fancy it.
games.players: 1 adult and 1 child, or pairs of children.
games.why_it_helps: Makes oral blending playful and gives a clear reason to hold sounds in mind and push them together.

games.name: Grapheme Treasure Hunt
games.gpc_focus: One target team per hunt, e.g. 'sh', 'ai' or 'igh'.
games.how_to_play: Hide grapheme cards (each showing one target team) around the room or garden. Call out the sound the child is hunting for, e.g. 'find the /sh/'. Children search, and each time they find a card they must say the sound and one word that contains it before it counts. Collect the whole set to open the (pretend) treasure box.
games.materials: Small cards with graphemes written on them; an optional box for the 'treasure'.
games.players: Small group works best; can be done solo.
games.why_it_helps: Adds movement and recall to grapheme recognition, which helps sounds stick.

games.name: First Sound Snapshot
games.gpc_focus: Initial sounds — pick a target sound the child is learning.
games.how_to_play: Lay out three or four picture cards. Say a target sound, e.g. 'point to the one that starts with /m/'. The child makes a 'camera' with their hands and 'snaps' a photo of the picture that begins with that sound, saying the word and the first sound aloud. Mix in one picture that starts with a similar sound to keep them listening carefully.
games.materials: Picture cards or real objects on a tray.
games.players: 1 child or a small group taking snaps in turn.
games.why_it_helps: Builds the skill of hearing and isolating the first sound in a word.

games.name: Tricky Word Bingo
games.gpc_focus: Tricky (common exception) words such as the, was, said, you, they.
games.how_to_play: Give each child a grid of six tricky words. The caller reads tricky words one at a time (and can pop each into a silly sentence). If a child has that word, they read it aloud and cover it with a counter. First to cover a full row calls 'Wren!' and reads their whole row back to win.
games.materials: Printed bingo grids and counters, or draw grids by hand.
games.why_it_helps: Builds fast, confident recognition of the words that can't simply be sounded out.

games.name: Rhyme Partners
games.gpc_focus: Rhyme and word families, e.g. -at, -ig, -op.
games.how_to_play: Spread out picture or word cards face up. Children take turns finding two cards that rhyme (cat and hat, dog and log) and saying both words to prove they rhyme. If the pair rhymes, they keep it; if not, the cards go back. Whoever collects the most rhyming pairs is the Rhyme Champion.
games.materials: A set of paired rhyming picture or word cards.
games.why_it_helps: Tunes the ear to the sounds at the end of words, a key early listening skill.

games.name: Sound Sorting Baskets
games.gpc_focus: Two sounds that are easy to muddle, e.g. /ee/ vs /oo/, or /f/ vs /v/.
games.how_to_play: Set out two baskets, each with a grapheme card on the front. Give the child a pile of picture or word cards. They say each word, listen for the target sound, and drop it in the matching basket. At the end, tip each basket out and read the words back together to check the sorting.
games.materials: Two baskets or hoops, grapheme labels, and word/picture cards.
games.players: 1 child or a small group sorting together.
games.why_it_helps: Sharpens listening for a specific sound and links it to its written team.

games.name: Real or Nonsense?
games.gpc_focus: Pure decoding of any taught GPCs, including made-up nonsense words.
games.how_to_play: Meet a little made-up creature who speaks in silly made-up words. Show a card with a decodable word on it — some are real words (bus, chip) and some are nonsense words (vosh, chab). The child sounds it out and blends it, then decides: is it a REAL word we put in the human box, or a NONSENSE word we beam back to the made-up creature? Both count as a win as long as they read it correctly.
games.materials: Cards with a mix of real and nonsense decodable words; two labelled boxes.
games.why_it_helps: Practises decoding for its own sake and mirrors the nonsense-word check used in the Year 1 phonics screening, without relying on already knowing the word.

games.name: Build-a-Sentence Strips
games.gpc_focus: Reading decodable words and tricky words together to make sense.
games.how_to_play: Give the child a jumble of word cards, including a few tricky words. They read each word, then slide the cards into an order that makes a real sentence, e.g. 'the cat sat on a mat'. Read the finished sentence back with a big storyteller voice. Add a full-stop card to finish. For a challenge, muddle a sentence and ask them to fix it.
games.materials: Word cards on card strips; a punctuation card or two.
games.why_it_helps: Bridges reading single words and reading for meaning across a whole sentence.

games.name: Sound Hopscotch
games.gpc_focus: Any set of taught graphemes chalked into the grid.
games.how_to_play: Chalk a hopscotch grid outside, writing one grapheme in each square instead of numbers. The child throws a beanbag onto a square, then hops to it saying each sound they land on along the way. When they reach the beanbag square, they say the sound and a word that uses it before hopping back.
games.materials: Chalk and a beanbag or small stone. An outdoor space.
games.players: 1 child or a queue of children taking turns.
games.why_it_helps: Links whole-body movement to sound recall, which many young children learn best through.

games.name: Sound-Walk Map
games.gpc_focus: None — a Phase 1 (Introduction) listening game played before any letters are taught.
games.how_to_play: Sit the children still in the garden or by an open window and ask them to close their eyes and just listen for one slow minute. When they open their eyes, draw a big circle on paper for 'here' and let each child name one sound they heard and roughly which direction it came from, and you dot it onto the map. Read the finished sound-map back together, pointing to each dot.
games.materials: A large sheet of paper and a pen. A spot to sit indoors or out.
games.why_it_helps: Trains children to tune out and then tune in to sounds on purpose, the very first listening skill.

games.name: What Made That Sound?
games.gpc_focus: None — a Phase 1 (Introduction) listening game played before any letters are taught.
games.how_to_play: Behind a low screen or a propped-up book, make one everyday sound out of sight — crunch a dry leaf, pour water into a cup, snap a twig, zip a coat. The children guess what made the sound before you lift the screen to show them. Let a child take a turn as the sound-maker once they get the idea.
games.materials: A screen or big book, and a tray of safe everyday objects that make a clear sound.
games.players: 1 adult with a small group; children can lead too.
games.why_it_helps: Sharpens careful listening and gives children the words to describe and compare sounds.

games.name: Beat Leader
games.format: Introduction — instrumental and body-percussion rhythm copying
games.gpc_focus: None — a Phase 1 (Introduction) listening game played before any letters are taught.
games.how_to_play: Sit in a circle with a drum, shakers or just knees to pat. One child is the Beat Leader and taps a short rhythm, such as tap-tap-rest-tap; everyone copies it straight back. When the group gets it right, that child picks the next leader and hands over the drum. Keep the patterns short at first and let them grow as children gain confidence.
games.materials: A drum, shakers or nothing at all — knees and hands work fine.
games.why_it_helps: Copying rhythms builds the memory for sound-patterns that later helps a child hold the sounds of a word in mind.

games.name: Rhyme Pot Soup
games.gpc_focus: None — a Phase 1 (Introduction) listening game played before any letters are taught.
games.how_to_play: Set a big pretend pot in the middle and give it a stir. Choose a starting word, say 'cat', then go round the circle with each child dropping in a word that rhymes with it — hat, mat, bat, even a made-up rhyming word. Give the pot a big stir and a pretend taste after every few words, and start a fresh pot with a new word when the rhymes run out.
games.materials: A pretend pot or a real bowl and a big wooden spoon.
games.why_it_helps: Thinking up rhymes, not just spotting them, is a strong sign a child is really hearing the ends of words.

games.name: Name and Snack
games.gpc_focus: None — a Phase 1 (Introduction) listening game played before any letters are taught.
games.how_to_play: Go round the group and help each child think of a pretend snack that starts with the same sound as their own name — 'Sam brings sausages', 'Priya brings pancakes', 'Tom brings toast'. Say the name and snack together with a clap on each matching starting sound. For a giggle, pile all the silly snacks onto one pretend plate at the end and 'eat' it together.
games.materials: None.
games.why_it_helps: Matching a starting sound to the most familiar word of all — a child's own name — makes the first sound in a word easy to hear.

games.name: Weather Voices
games.gpc_focus: None — a Phase 1 (Introduction) listening game played before any letters are taught.
games.how_to_play: Hold up simple weather pictures one at a time and let the children make each weather with their voices — a long 'whoooo' for wind, a soft 'pit-pit-pit' for rain, a low rumbling 'boom' for thunder, a bright 'ahh' for sunshine. Mix the pictures faster and slower, louder and quieter, so voices swoop up and down. Finish on a calm sunny 'ahh' to settle everyone.
games.materials: A few simple weather picture cards.
games.why_it_helps: Playing with the voice — high and low, long and short, loud and quiet — is the groundwork for making and shaping speech sounds.

games.name: Bolt's Sound Fetch
games.format: Introduction — oral blending (Bolt the Robot mascot)
games.gpc_focus: None — a Phase 1 oral-blending game; sounds are spoken aloud, no letters are shown.
games.how_to_play: Bolt is a friendly little robot whose rusty voice can only say things in separate sounds. Lay out a few real objects with short names — a cup, a hat, a pen, a sock. Bolt (you) asks for one in sounds, 'please pass the c-u-p', and the children blend the sounds in their heads and fetch the right object. Let a child be Bolt and robot-talk the next object once they have the hang of it.
games.materials: A handful of familiar objects with short names.
games.why_it_helps: Blending spoken sounds into a whole word by ear is the exact skill a child will later use to read, practised here with no letters in sight.

games.name: Sound Steps
games.gpc_focus: None — a Phase 1 oral-segmenting game; sounds are spoken aloud, no letters are shown.
games.how_to_play: Stand at one end of the room or garden. Say a short word out loud, such as 'dog', then break it into its sounds together — d ... o ... g — taking one big step forward for each sound. Count how many steps the word took to cross the room. Try longer words like 'frog' or 'plant' and see which words carry you furthest.
games.materials: A clear space to walk across.
games.players: 1 child or a small group stepping together.
games.why_it_helps: Breaking a spoken word into its separate sounds — one step each — builds segmenting, the skill a child needs for spelling.

games.name: Digraph Detective
games.gpc_focus: Two-letter teams (digraphs) such as sh, ch, th, ng, ai, ee, oa, oo.
games.how_to_play: Give the child a magnifying glass (a real one or a pretend circle made with finger and thumb) and a few short words written large, each hiding one two-letter team. They hunt through each word, loop around the team when they spot it, and say the one sound those two letters make together. Cheer each solved case and move the detective on to the next word.
games.materials: Words written on paper or a whiteboard; an optional toy magnifying glass.
games.players: 1 child or a small group taking turns as the detective.
games.why_it_helps: Trains children to see two letters as a single sound, which stops them sounding digraphs out letter by letter.

games.name: Sneaky-e Swap
games.gpc_focus: Split digraphs a-e, i-e, o-e, u-e and e-e — the 'sneaky e' that reaches back to change a vowel.
games.how_to_play: Write a short word the child can already read, such as 'tap', 'pin', 'cub' or 'not', and read it together. Then slide a card with a lower-case e onto the end and explain that this sneaky e quietly reaches back over one letter and makes the vowel say its name — 'tap' becomes 'tape', 'pin' becomes 'pine', 'cub' becomes 'cube'. Read the new word together and talk about how the middle sound changed.
games.materials: Word cards or a whiteboard, plus a few loose 'e' cards.
games.why_it_helps: Shows children how a split digraph works by watching a familiar word transform, rather than meeting the pattern cold.

games.name: Tricky Word Treasure
games.gpc_focus: Tricky (common exception) words such as the, was, said, you, they, one and when.
games.how_to_play: Write tricky words on paper 'gems' or 'coins' and scatter them around the room or bury them in a tray of sand or dry pasta. A child digs or searches for a gem, reads the tricky word on it aloud, and only then may drop it into the treasure chest. When the chest is full, tip it out and read the whole hoard back together.
games.materials: Paper gems or coins with tricky words on; a box for the chest; an optional tray of sand or pasta.
games.why_it_helps: Adds movement and repetition to the words that can't be sounded out, building fast recognition on sight.

games.name: Phrase Race
games.gpc_focus: Reading short decodable phrases smoothly, blending taught GPCs and tricky words at speed.
games.how_to_play: Write four or five short decodable phrases on strips, such as 'a red hen', 'up the tall hill', 'down to the sea'. Turn a sand-timer or count softly while the child reads the whole set aloud as smoothly as they can, aiming to beat their own last go rather than anyone else. Praise smooth, joined-up reading more than pure speed, and re-read any phrase that came out bumpy.
games.materials: Phrase strips and a sand-timer or a quiet count.
games.players: 1 child, or pairs cheering each other on.
games.why_it_helps: Moves children on from sounding out single words to reading groups of words smoothly, which is what reading for meaning needs.

games.name: Grapheme-Picture Match
games.gpc_focus: Matching a grapheme to a word that contains that sound — ai/rain, ee/tree, oa/goat, sh/fish.
games.how_to_play: Lay out grapheme cards in one row and picture cards jumbled in a row below. The child picks a picture, says its name aloud, listens for the target sound inside it, and lays it next to the matching grapheme card. Keep going until every picture sits beside its sound, then read each pair back together to check.
games.materials: Grapheme cards and matching picture cards.
games.players: 1 child or a small group matching together.
games.why_it_helps: Links the written team to a real word children can picture, cementing what sound each grapheme stands for.

games.name: Sentence Swap
games.gpc_focus: Reading a whole decodable sentence and noticing how swapping one word changes the meaning.
games.how_to_play: Build a simple decodable sentence from word cards, such as 'the big dog ran fast', and read it together. Then swap just one word card for another — 'big' for 'red', 'dog' for 'cat', 'fast' for 'home' — and read the brand-new sentence aloud. Let the child choose which word to swap, and the sillier the sentence gets the better.
games.materials: A set of decodable word cards, including a few spares to swap in.
games.why_it_helps: Shows children that reading is about meaning — change one word and the whole picture in your head changes.
